questions.question:
Analyze the compile-time behavior of this dynamic invocation:
dynamic value = 10;
value.DoNotExitMethod();

options.label: B
options.text: It compiles successfully but will throw a RuntimeBinderException at runtime

options.label: C
options.text: It compiles and runs successfully, returning null

questions.explanation: The `dynamic` type bypasses compile-time checks. The compiler accepts the method call, but at runtime, the Binder fails to find `DoNotExitMethod` on the integer value, throwing `RuntimeBinderException`.
questions.hint: Dynamic types defer binding to runtime; the compiler trust that the method exists.

options.label: D
options.text: Compiler Error: Struct assignment is prohibited

questions.explanation: In C#, structs are value types. Assigning `p1` to `p2` copies the entire data of the struct. Modifying `p2.x` does not affect `p1.x`.
questions.hint: Value types copy the actual data to a new location on the stack.

options.label: D
options.text: Compiler Error: Class assignment is prohibited

questions.explanation: Classes are reference types. Assigning `p1` to `p2` copies the reference pointing to the same heap-allocated object. Modifying `p2.x` affects `p1.x`.
questions.hint: Reference types copy reference pointers to the same heap memory object.

questions.question: What is the default value of a reference type variable declared inside a C# class before it is assigned?
questions.explanation: All C# reference types default to `null` before a concrete instance is assigned.
questions.hint: Value types default to 0/false; reference types default to empty references.

questions.question: What is the default value of the fields in the following struct upon invoking parameterless creation? `struct Item { public int count; public bool isSold; }`

options.label: C
options.text: Compiler Error: Parameterless creation is illegal

questions.explanation: Struct value types automatically initialize their fields to their respective default values (0 for numerical types, false for booleans) when constructed.
questions.hint: All fields are zero-initialized by the runtime.

questions.question: The C# data type `int` is an alias for which System type?
questions.explanation: In C#, predefined types are aliases for System-provided types. `int` is a direct alias for `System.Int32`.
questions.hint: An int represents a 32-bit signed integer.

questions.question: How many bits are allocated for a C# `char` variable, and what character set does it support?
questions.explanation: C# `char` represents a single UTF-16 Unicode character, which is allocated 16 bits in memory.
questions.hint: Think about internationalization support in C#.

questions.question: Which of the following C# parameter modifiers is used to denote optional parameters, and where must they be declared?

options.label: A
options.text: By providing a default value, e.g., 'int x = 5'; they must be declared at the end of the parameter list.

options.label: B
options.text: Using the 'optional' keyword; they can be declared anywhere in the signature.

options.label: C
options.text: Using 'params'; they must be declared at the beginning.

options.label: D
options.text: By adding '?' after the type; they can appear in any position.

questions.explanation: Optional parameters are defined by assigning default values in the method signature. They must appear after all required parameters.
questions.hint: Optional parameters cannot be placed before required ones.

questions.question: What compile-time constraint exists when using the C# `out` keyword?

options.label: A
options.text: The callee method must assign a value to the parameter before returning normally.

options.label: B
options.text: The caller must assign a non-null value before passing.

options.label: C
options.text: The parameter must be of reference type.

questions.explanation: When a parameter is marked with `out`, the C# compiler enforces a rule that the method must assign a value to that parameter before leaving the method scope.
questions.hint: The callee is obligated to assign a value to out variables.

questions.question: Which of the following C# types is a reference type allocated on the heap?
questions.explanation: Strings, classes, interfaces, and delegates are reference types allocated on the heap. Integers, booleans, and enums are value types.
questions.hint: Strings in C# behave like objects with reference storage.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of Encapsulation in object-oriented design?

options.label: A
options.text: To allow classes to inherit methods from each other.

options.label: B
options.text: To protect sensitive data from direct outside manipulation by bundling data and methods together.

options.label: C
options.text: To enable multiple methods to share the same name but different signatures.

options.label: D
options.text: To compile classes in separate assemblies.

questions.explanation: Encapsulation prevents unauthorized access or modification of an object's internal state, controlling access via getters, setters, and properties.
questions.hint: Encapsulation is also known as information hiding.

questions.explanation: Using properties encapsulates private fields, allowing validation during value assignment. Since -5 is invalid, the setter defaults it to 1.0.
questions.hint: Properties allow custom setter logic.

questions.question: Which of the following is true for constructors in C#?

options.label: B
options.text: They must have the exact same name as the class and declare no return type.

options.label: C
options.text: They can be called manually at any time on an existing object.

options.label: D
options.text: They can be marked as abstract.

questions.explanation: Constructors prepare an object upon creation. They have no return type (not even void) and share the name of the containing class.
questions.hint: Constructors run once automatically during instantiation.

questions.question: In C#, how do you specify that a derived constructor should execute a specific base class constructor first?

options.label: A
options.text: By calling base() inside the method body.

options.label: B
options.text: By adding ': base()' or ': base(arguments)' after the constructor declaration.

options.label: D
options.text: By calling base.Constructor() in the first line.

questions.explanation: The `: base(...)` initializer is used to call a specific constructor in the parent class before executing the derived constructor's body.
questions.hint: It appears in the constructor signature declaration line, after a colon.

questions.question: What does applying the sealed modifier to a C# class accomplish?

options.label: A
options.text: It prevents the class from being instantiated.

options.label: B
options.text: It prevents the class from being inherited by other classes.

options.label: C
options.text: It forces all class members to be static.

options.label: D
options.text: It restricts accessibility to the same file.

questions.explanation: Sealed classes prevent other classes from inheriting from them. This is useful for security, performance optimizations, and keeping classes self-contained.
questions.hint: Sealing a class stops others from subclassing it.

questions.hint: Method hiding resolves to the reference type's class, not the runtime object type.

questions.explanation: Because `Print` is virtual and overridden in the child, C# uses runtime dynamic dispatch (via the Virtual Method Table) to call the overridden method of the runtime object type, yielding 'C'.
questions.hint: Virtual overriding resolves calls to the actual runtime object instance.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding **Abstract Classes** in C#?

options.label: A
options.text: They cannot contain concrete methods with implementations.

options.label: B
options.text: They cannot be instantiated directly using 'new'.

options.label: C
options.text: They must have only abstract methods.

options.label: D
options.text: They support multiple inheritance in C#.

questions.explanation: Abstract classes serve as templates and cannot be instantiated directly. However, unlike interfaces, they can contain concrete methods with code logic.
questions.hint: Abstract classes define a common subclass template but cannot be constructed directly.

questions.question: Why does C# disallow multiple inheritance of classes but allow implementing multiple interfaces?

options.label: A
options.text: To prevent name collisions and diamond dependency conflicts arising from multiple parents sharing concrete code.

options.label: B
options.text: Because interfaces do not use memory on the stack.

options.label: C
options.text: Because classes are value types, while interfaces are reference types.

questions.explanation: Allowing a class to inherit from multiple parents with different concrete implementations can lead to structural ambiguities (the diamond problem). Interfaces only define contracts without state, avoiding this issue.
questions.hint: Multiple inheritance of concrete code creates method definition ambiguities.

questions.question: Which term describes a composition relationship where the child object **cannot** exist independently of the parent object's lifecycle?
questions.explanation: In strong composition (often just called Composition), the parent object owns the lifecycle of the child object. If the parent is destroyed, the child is destroyed too.
questions.hint: Aggregation is weak composition; this is the strong variant.

questions.question: Analyze this class relationship. An `Enrollment` class contains a reference to `Student` and `Course` instances. If the `Enrollment` instance is deleted, the `Student` and `Course` still exist. What type of composition relationship is this?
questions.explanation: Aggregation represents a weak 'has-a' relationship where the contained objects have lifecycles independent of the container object.
questions.hint: Contained items outlive the container in this relationship.

questions.question: What is the difference between Implementation Inheritance and Definition Inheritance?

options.label: A
options.text: Implementation inheritance uses interfaces; definition inheritance uses base classes.

options.label: B
options.text: Implementation inheritance inherits actual code behavior from a base class; definition inheritance inherits method contracts from an interface.

options.label: C
options.text: Implementation inheritance is value type based; definition inheritance is reference type based.

questions.explanation: Class inheritance provides implementation inheritance (inheriting base code), while interface implementation provides definition inheritance (complying with a method contract).
questions.hint: Think about class extension vs interface contracts.

questions.question: Which access modifier restricts visibility to only within the same class and any class derived from it?
questions.explanation: The `protected` access modifier allows visibility within the declaring class and its subclasses, denying access to unrelated classes.
questions.hint: This modifier is critical for subclass implementation sharing.

questions.question: What is the visibility boundary of the internal access modifier in C#?

options.label: A
options.text: Visible only within the same class.

options.label: B
options.text: Visible within the same project assembly.

options.label: C
options.text: Visible to any class in any assembly.

questions.explanation: Types or members marked as `internal` are accessible only within files of the same assembly (compilation output, like a DLL or EXE).
questions.hint: Internal restricts access to the containing assembly.

questions.question: Which principle is represented by: 'Favor Composition over Inheritance'?

options.label: A
options.text: Achieving flexibility by using has-a relationships to delegate behavior at runtime instead of static is-a trees.

options.label: B
options.text: Eliminating interfaces to reduce class counts.

options.label: C
options.text: Using multiple base classes in C#.

questions.explanation: Composition allows objects to dynamically refer to different implementations at runtime, whereas inheritance binds behaviors statically at compile-time.
questions.hint: Dynamic association is more flexible than static inheritance hierarchies.

questions.question: In C#, what is the difference between a parameterless constructor and an automatic parameterless constructor generated by the compiler?

options.label: A
options.text: There is no functional difference; the compiler-generated constructor runs if no custom constructors are defined, initializing fields to defaults.

options.label: B
options.text: The compiler-generated constructor allocates memory on the stack instead of the heap.

options.label: C
options.text: The custom constructor cannot be overloaded.

options.label: D
options.text: The compiler-generated constructor forces the class to be static.

questions.explanation: If a class does not define any constructors, the compiler automatically generates a public, parameterless constructor that initializes all fields to their default values.
questions.hint: The compiler steps in only if you write no constructors.

questions.question: Can a constructor in C# call another overloaded constructor of the same class, and if so, how?

options.label: A
options.text: No, constructors cannot call each other.

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, by adding ': this(arguments)' after the constructor declaration.

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, by calling this.Constructor() in the first line of the body.

questions.explanation: Using `: this(...)` in the constructor declaration delegates initialization to another constructor of the same class before executing the constructor's body.
questions.hint: This is constructor chaining within the same class using a keyword.

questions.question: What is the runtime dispatch result when calling an abstract method on a base class reference containing a derived object instance?

options.label: A
options.text: It resolves to the derived class override implementation at runtime.

options.label: C
options.text: It invokes a blank base method.

questions.explanation: Abstract methods have no body and are implicitly virtual. Runtime dispatch resolves them to the concrete override in the instantiated subclass.
questions.hint: Abstract methods behave like virtual methods with no default implementation.

questions.question: Which OOP concept is defined as: 'Exposing only the necessary public API interface while hiding internal implementation details'?
questions.explanation: Abstraction isolates implementation details behind a clean conceptual contract (like an interface or abstract class), reducing overall system complexity.
questions.hint: Detail hiding is Abstraction; data hiding is Encapsulation.

questions.question: If Class A has a field of type Class B, and Class B is used as a service helper, what is the conceptual relationship between A and B?
questions.explanation: Having a reference to another class as a member establishes a 'has-a' relationship (Composition or Aggregation) rather than an 'is-a' relationship (Inheritance).
questions.hint: Containing another object represents ownership or association.

options.label: D
options.text: Only if the Facade is marked as static.

questions.explanation: Facades promote weak coupling. Subsystem classes remain public, allowing advanced clients to bypass the facade when necessary.
questions.hint: A facade simplifies access but does not lock or hide the subsystem classes.

questions.question: [EXAMINE DIAGRAM] In the Secure Access (Proxy) UML structure, why does `ProxySubject` implement the `Subject` interface?

options.label: A
options.text: To allow client code to interact with ProxySubject interchangeably with RealSubject, following polymorphism.

options.label: D
options.text: To convert reference types to values.

questions.explanation: A proxy must share the same interface as the real subject, allowing clients to pass the proxy transparently without modifying client code.
questions.hint: Sharing an interface allows polymorphically substituting the proxy for the real object.

questions.question: Which proxy type is designed to delay expensive initialization (like loading large images or database records) until the object is actually used?
questions.explanation: A Virtual Proxy (Lazy Proxy) manages initialization of expensive resources, instantiating the real subject only when a method is called.
questions.hint: This proxy delays resource allocation until the last second.

questions.question: Which proxy type validates client authentication details before delegating requests to the underlying object?
questions.explanation: A Protection Proxy acts as a security gatekeeper, checking credentials and permissions before granting access to the RealSubject.
questions.hint: This proxy protects the real object by verifying permissions first.

questions.question: [EXAMINE DIAGRAM] In the Adapter pattern diagram, what is the role of the `Adapter` class?

options.label: A
options.text: It implements the target interface, and translates calls to the incompatible adaptee class using composition.

options.label: B
options.text: It inherits from client classes directly.

options.label: C
options.text: It compiles legacy code into C# assembly.

questions.explanation: The `Adapter` implements the interface the client expects (`Target`) and translates requests into a format the legacy class (`Adaptee`) understands.
questions.hint: Look for the class bridging the Target and Adaptee.

questions.question: What is the key difference between the intent of the Adapter pattern and the Facade pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: Adapter changes interfaces to enable compatibility; Facade simplifies interfaces to reduce complexity.

options.label: B
options.text: Adapter is creational; Facade is behavioral.

options.label: C
options.text: Adapter uses inheritance; Facade uses composition only.

questions.explanation: Adapter bridges two incompatible interfaces. Facade creates a new, simplified interface to wrap a complex group of classes.
questions.hint: Think compatibility (Adapter) vs simplification (Facade).

questions.question: What is the primary objective of the Decorator design pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: To prevent classes from overriding base methods.

options.label: B
options.text: To attach additional behaviors and responsibilities to objects dynamically at runtime without subclassing.

options.label: C
options.text: To convert interfaces to match client expectations.

options.label: D
options.text: To allocate memory directly on the stack.

questions.explanation: Decorator wraps concrete components, adding behaviors (like scrollbars to window objects) at runtime without altering the class hierarchy.
questions.hint: This pattern is a flexible alternative to subclassing.

questions.question: Why does a Decorator class inherit the interface of the component it decorates, while also holding a reference to an instance of it?

options.label: A
options.text: To satisfy C# compiler naming rules.

options.label: B
options.text: To conform to the contract (allowing transparent nesting) while delegating operations to the wrapped instance.

questions.explanation: Inheriting the interface allows the decorated object to be used interchangeably with undecorated ones. Holding a reference allows it to delegate calls to the wrapped object.
questions.hint: Interchangeability (inheritance) + delegation (reference composition).

questions.question: [EXAMINE DIAGRAM] In the File/Folder Composite structure, how does the Composite pattern enable uniform treatment of files and folders?

options.label: B
options.text: By making both implement the Component interface, allowing client code to call `Display()` on both uniformly.

questions.explanation: Composite allows clients to treat individual objects (`File`) and compositions (`Folder`) uniformly using a common base type interface.
questions.hint: Uniform treatment comes from both inheriting from the Component base class.

questions.question: What is the primary design trade-off between Uniformity and Safety in the Composite pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: Uniformity places child management methods (Add/Remove) in the base Component, risking errors on Leaf nodes. Safety places them only in Composite, requiring casting.

options.label: B
options.text: Uniformity is value type based; Safety is reference type based.

options.label: C
options.text: Uniformity speeds up compiles; Safety speeds up execution.

questions.explanation: Declaring child management (Add/Remove) in `Component` provides uniformity (all nodes look the same) but sacrifices safety because calling `Add` on a `File` throws a runtime exception.
questions.hint: Think about what happens if you call Add(child) on a simple Leaf file.

questions.question: What is the difference between an Object Adapter and a Class Adapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Object Adapter uses composition to wrap the adaptee; Class Adapter uses multiple inheritance (inheriting both Target and Adaptee).

options.label: B
options.text: Object Adapter resides on the stack; Class Adapter on the heap.

options.label: D
options.text: Class Adapter is creational; Object Adapter is structural.

questions.explanation: Object Adapter references the adaptee instance at runtime (composition). Class Adapter inherits from the Adaptee class directly, which requires multiple inheritance support.
questions.hint: Think delegation via pointer vs inheritance of multiple classes.

questions.question: Which of the following contains ONLY structural design patterns?
questions.explanation: Facade, Proxy, Adapter, Decorator, and Composite are GoF structural patterns, concerned with class and object composition.
questions.hint: Structural patterns focus on combining classes and objects into larger structures.

questions.question: Why is the Decorator pattern preferred over subclassing in systems with many optional features?

options.label: A
options.text: Subclassing optional feature combinations leads to a combinatorial class explosion (e.g. 128 subclasses for 7 options). Decorator stacks components dynamically.

options.label: B
options.text: Because Decorators reside on the stack.

options.label: C
options.text: Because subclassing is prohibited in C#.

options.label: D
options.text: Decorator has no benefits over subclassing.

questions.explanation: Subclassing combinations creates a combinatorial explosion. Stacking decorators at runtime keeps class counts low and code maintainable.
questions.hint: Stacking optional wrappers at runtime avoids class definition explosions.

questions.question: What is the key difference in intent between the Proxy pattern and the Decorator pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: Proxy controls access to a subject; Decorator adds behaviors to a subject.

options.label: B
options.text: Proxy is creational; Decorator is behavioral.

options.label: C
options.text: Proxy uses class inheritance; Decorator uses interfaces.

questions.explanation: Proxy represents the real object to manage its access or lifetime. Decorator wraps the object to extend its features dynamically.
questions.hint: Access control (Proxy) vs enhancement (Decorator).

questions.question: How does introducing a Facade affect coupling between client code and subsystem components?

options.label: B
options.text: It promotes weak coupling, isolating changes in the subsystem from the client.

questions.explanation: The client only couples to the Facade class, decoupling it from the numerous, evolving subsystem class APIs.
questions.hint: Facade acts as an isolation barrier for client code.

questions.question: In distributed systems, which proxy type acts as a local representative for an object that resides in a different address space or server?
questions.explanation: A Remote Proxy handles networking details (serializing requests, sending packets) to make remote objects look local to the client.
questions.hint: Think representing server objects locally.

questions.question: What is the defining characteristic of a Leaf node in the Composite pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: It contains child elements and manages their lifecycles.

options.label: B
options.text: It has no children and defines the primitive, basic behaviors of the composition.

questions.explanation: Leaf nodes represent the basic building blocks that do not contain child elements (e.g. `File` in a file system).
questions.hint: Leaves are terminal nodes with no descendants.

questions.question: What is the role of the `Target` interface in the Adapter pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: It defines the domain-specific interface that the client code expects and uses.

options.label: B
options.text: It is the legacy class being adapted.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the main database engine class.

questions.explanation: The Target interface is the common contract client code expects. The Adapter implements Target, bridging to the Adaptee.
questions.hint: The interface the client uses is the Target.

questions.question: How does using Facades support layering in software architecture?

options.label: A
options.text: By allowing layers to bypass each other.

options.label: B
options.text: By defining a clean, simplified entry point for each layer to communicate with the layer below it, minimizing inter-layer dependencies.

options.label: C
options.text: By merging all layers into one file.

questions.explanation: Each tier in an architecture can expose a Facade as its public gatekeeper API, ensuring other tiers only communicate via simple interfaces.
questions.hint: Entry points for layer-to-layer communication.

questions.question: [EXAMINE DIAGRAM] In the Discount Chain of Responsibility case study, how does this pattern resolve SRP and coupling smells?

options.label: A
options.text: By packing all rules into a single class with if-else logic.

options.label: B
options.text: By dividing conditions into discrete, independent handler classes (`HighDiscountHandler`, `MediumDiscountHandler`) linked together, satisfying SRP and OCP.

questions.explanation: COR encapsulates separate handler conditions in separate classes. Senders don't know which class handles the request, minimizing coupling.
questions.hint: Look for how the handlers are split and chained together.

questions.question: What happens in a Chain of Responsibility if no handler in the chain satisfies the request's condition?

options.label: B
options.text: The request falls off the end of the chain, returning a default value or leaving the request unhandled without crashing.

options.label: C
options.text: The application enters an infinite loop.

questions.explanation: If the end of the chain is reached (`nextHandler == null`) without processing, the system returns a default fallback state or logs it as unhandled.
questions.hint: Think about what happens if nextHandler is null and nothing matched.

questions.question: In the Chain of Responsibility, how do handlers route requests to the next element in the chain?

options.label: A
options.text: By calling a static class method directly.

options.label: B
options.text: By invoking the `Handle` method on the reference to the next handler (`_nextHandler.Handle(amount)`) if it is not null.

questions.explanation: Each handler holds a reference to the next object in the chain and invokes its methods to forward the request dynamically.
questions.hint: Communication is done by passing the request to the next handler reference.

questions.question: What is the primary objective of the Strategy pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: To ensure a class has only a single instance.

options.label: B
options.text: To define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable at runtime using composition.

options.label: C
options.text: To route requests along a chain of handlers.

questions.explanation: Strategy extracts algorithmic variations into strategy classes, allowing the client to swap them dynamically.
questions.hint: Interchangeable algorithms using composition point to this pattern.

questions.question: What is a key difference in usage between the Strategy pattern and the State pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: Strategy is creational; State is structural.

options.label: B
options.text: Strategy algorithms are usually configured once and are independent; State objects transition from one state to another dynamically based on context inputs.

options.label: C
options.text: Strategy uses inheritance; State uses interfaces only.

questions.explanation: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms. State encapsulates behaviors tied to internal states that transition dynamically.
questions.hint: Static choice of algorithm (Strategy) vs dynamic phase transitions (State).

questions.question: In the WeatherStation Observer case study, how does `WeatherStation` notify interested displays?

options.label: B
options.text: By looping over a list of registered `IObserver` interface instances and invoking their `Update()` method, decoupling the subject from concrete display types.

options.label: C
options.text: By writing data to a shared database.

questions.explanation: Subject tracks observers using the interface `IObserver`. When a change occurs, it notifies them polylmorphically, staying decoupled from concrete display types.
questions.hint: Decoupling is achieved by iterating over an interface collection.

questions.question: What does 'Loose Coupling' mean in the context of the Observer pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: The Subject does not need to know the concrete classes of its Observers; it only interacts via the IObserver interface contract.

options.label: B
options.text: Observers reside on the stack, and the subject resides on the heap.

options.label: C
options.text: The classes can compile without assembly references.

questions.explanation: Because the Subject only knows `IObserver`, new observer classes can be registered without modifying the Subject class.
questions.hint: Think about why the Weather Station doesn't crash when adding a smartwatch display.

questions.question: In a Smart Home IoT (Command Pattern) system, what is the role of a `LightOnCommand` class?

options.label: A
options.text: It is the receiver object that performs the actual light operations.

options.label: B
options.text: It encapsulates the light receiver and implements the ICommand interface, invoking `receiver.TurnOn()` inside its `Execute()` method.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the remote control button class.

questions.explanation: The Command class wraps the receiver (`Light`) and its specific action (`TurnOn()`), exposing it as a uniform `Execute()` contract to the invoker.
questions.hint: The concrete command coordinates the receiver and the action.

questions.question: How does the Command pattern support undo operations in a text editor?

options.label: B
options.text: By storing executed commands in a history stack and invoking their `Undo()` method, which performs the reverse operation or restores cached state.

options.label: C
options.text: By calling the garbage collector to roll back heap state.

questions.explanation: Because commands are objects, they can store execution context. Keeping them in a stack allows running their corresponding `Undo()` operations in reverse order.
questions.hint: Object-oriented actions can easily be saved to a history list.

questions.question: Which interface in the C# .NET framework represents the Iterator design pattern?
questions.explanation: The `IEnumerator` and `IEnumerable` interfaces provide standard iteration methods (`MoveNext`, `Current`), encapsulating collection traversals.
questions.hint: This interface enables 'foreach' loop support in C#.

questions.question: What is the primary characteristic of the Template Method pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: It uses generic parameters to compile methods.

options.label: B
options.text: It defines the structural steps of an algorithm in a base class method, letting subclasses override specific steps without changing the overall algorithm structure.

options.label: D
options.text: It routes requests along a chain.

questions.explanation: Template Method establishes the algorithm skeleton in a base method. Subclasses override specific hook methods to insert details without altering execution flow.
questions.hint: Skeletal algorithm steps in base; step details overridden in children.

questions.question: What is the primary objective of the Visitor pattern?

options.label: B
options.text: To define new operations on elements of an object structure without modifying the element classes themselves, using double dispatch.

options.label: C
options.text: To wrap complex subsystems behind a facade.

questions.explanation: Visitor separates operations from object structures. Elements accept a visitor, delegating execution to the visitor class (double dispatch).
questions.hint: Adding operations without modifying the structure classes.

questions.question: Which of the following contains ONLY behavioral design patterns?

options.label: B
options.text: Chain of Responsibility, Strategy, Observer, Command

questions.explanation: Chain of Responsibility, Strategy, Observer, and Command are behavioral patterns, concerned with object communication and delegation.
questions.hint: Behavioral patterns focus on dynamic communication and logic routing.

questions.question: What is the primary intent of the Memento pattern?

options.label: B
options.text: To capture and externalize an object's internal state without violating encapsulation, allowing the object to be restored to this state later.

questions.explanation: Memento saves snapshots of object states privately, allowing restoration (undo) while keeping internal fields hidden from outside classes.
questions.hint: Encapsulated state snapshots for restore operations.

questions.question: What problem is solved by the Mediator design pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: The need to create complex objects step-by-step.

options.label: B
options.text: Tight coupling and chaotic direct dependencies among a set of collaborating objects, routing all communications through a central mediator instead.

questions.explanation: Mediator encapsulates how objects interact. Instead of objects referencing each other directly, they only reference the Mediator, reducing coupling.
questions.hint: Centralizing communication among peers to prevent direct coupling.

questions.question: How does the Strategy pattern support the Open/Closed Principle?

options.label: B
options.text: By allowing new algorithm strategies to be added without modifying the context class that uses the strategies.

questions.explanation: Strategy uses interface composition. We can add new strategies (extension) without modifying the client class (closed for modification).
questions.hint: Adding strategies does not edit the client processor.

questions.question: How do Chain of Responsibility and Command differ in request routing?

options.label: A
options.text: COR delegates the request dynamically along a chain of potential handlers; Command binds a request to a specific receiver action in a single object.

options.label: B
options.text: COR is creational; Command is structural.

options.label: C
options.text: COR requires database persistence; Command is stack-based.

questions.explanation: COR is dynamic and open-ended: any handler in the chain might process the request. Command is direct: it encapsulates a specific action on a specific receiver.
questions.hint: Open-ended routing along links vs explicit action encapsulation.

questions.question: Under what condition is the Interpreter pattern recommended?

options.label: B
options.text: When a problem occurs frequently and can be expressed as a simple sentence in a defined grammar that can be parsed as an abstract syntax tree.

questions.explanation: Interpreter represents grammar rules as classes, resolving simple language sentences by parsing them into syntax tree objects.
questions.hint: Grammar rules represented as class structures.

questions.question: In the State pattern, where is the logic for transitioning from one state to another typically defined?

options.label: A
options.text: Only in the client UI code.

options.label: B
options.text: Either inside the context class or within the concrete state subclasses, depending on whether transitions are static or dynamic.

questions.explanation: State transitions can be managed by the Context for simple structures, or delegated to state classes for dynamic, data-driven transitions.
questions.hint: Transitions can reside in the context orchestrator or the state steps themselves.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Push Model and the Pull Model in the Observer pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: Push Model sends detailed state data in the update call; Pull Model only notifies observers, which then query the subject for the specific data they need.

options.label: B
options.text: Push Model uses value types; Pull Model uses reference types.

options.label: C
options.text: Push Model is asynchronous; Pull Model is synchronous.

options.label: D
options.text: Push Model is structural; Pull Model is creational.

questions.explanation: Push model sends change details directly to observers (tight coupling to payload). Pull model sends a simple notification, letting observers fetch what they want.
questions.hint: Broadcasting the detailed data vs sending a notification requiring a query.

The ability of different objects to respond to the same message with unique behaviors (same name, different behaviors).

Modeling real-world concepts in code by hiding implementation complexity and exposing a clean interface.
